clue.text: Bishop talks about some fish, but he won't catch much

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word wraps the other here

parts.note: utters means speaks or talks
a finger of fish, as in a fish finger, is a portion of fish

explanation.surface: A clergyman chats about fish but is a poor angler who never lands anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts one piece around the other, after B. The fishing surface hides the cricket sense: a fielder who catches little.
explanation.definitionFit: A butterfingers is a clumsy person who keeps dropping things, notably a fielder who fumbles chances.

clue.text: Joining train to Winchester, perhaps

parts.note: boarding a vehicle is getting on or joining it
to school someone is to train or teach them

explanation.surface: A traveller catches a train bound for the city of Winchester.
explanation.walkthrough: 'train' reads as the railway noun but is the verb, to school. Winchester College is a famous English residential public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Winchester College is a famous example of a residential school where pupils live during term.

clue.text: Trunk growing from gnarled roots

indicators.note: gnarled means twisted and knotted, so the letters of the next word are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A tree trunk rises from its knotted, twisted roots.
explanation.definitionFit: The trunk is the body without head and limbs, the torso, here disguised as a tree's trunk.

clue.text: Speed of enterprise

definitions.meaning: speed in the sense of promptness or dispatch in doing something
an enterprise is a venture or organised journey with a purpose

explanation.definitionFit: Expedition means both haste in getting things done and a journey undertaken for a purpose, a venture.

clue.text: Leaves page unfinished — three footnotes to be added

indicators.note: unfinished means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a folio is a numbered leaf or page of a book
three musical notes, A, G and E, added at the foot or end

explanation.surface: An incomplete page needs three footnotes appended before it is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' cuts the last letter from FOLIO to give FOLI. 'footnotes' looks like scholarly notes but means notes (A, G, E) at the foot, as 'to be added' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: The leaves of a plant taken together make up its greenery, so the plural noun matches.

clue.text: Pet scheme for a number to play the guitar

parts.note: to strum is to play a guitar by sweeping the strings

explanation.surface: Someone's favourite plan is to strum a song on the guitar.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a favourite remedy or scheme, often a quack cure, that someone keeps promoting.

clue.text: Moderate affluence

definitions.meaning: to moderate is to lessen or relieve, as pain
affluence as comfortable wealth, a life of comfort

explanation.definitionFit: To ease pain is to moderate it, and a life of ease is one of comfortable wealth.

clue.text: Made notes about every point requiring alteration

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: singers make musical notes, so this is sang
each means every one
E is a compass point, east

explanation.surface: Someone revised their notes on every point that needed changing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the singing word round every. 'Made notes' looks like jotting things down; it is singing.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea change is a profound transformation, a phrase taken from Shakespeare's The Tempest.

clue.text: Deceased's title should keep the line safe

parts.note: a dead man's, belonging to someone who has died
a handle is slang for a name or title

explanation.surface: A dead person's title should keep a family line secure.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'line' is a railway line: the device stops the train if the driver lets go.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead man's handle is a safety control on trains that halts the engine if the driver collapses.

clue.text: Kremlin reverses missile emplacement after a cut

indicators.note: after places the reversed piece behind the words a and cut

parts.note: to crop is to cut short

indicators.note: reverses means the piece for the missile emplacement is read backwards

parts.note: a silo is an underground housing for a missile

explanation.surface: Moscow's government backs down on a missile site after budget cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverses' turns the missile site into OLIS. 'Kremlin' looks like the subject of the sentence but is the definition: it is Moscow's citadel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kremlin is Moscow's citadel, and an acropolis is the fortified high citadel of a Greek city.

clue.text: Quench dryness at last with water

indicators.note: at last means take the final letter of the word dryness

parts.note: a lake is a body of water

explanation.surface: Someone finally cures their thirst with a drink of water.
explanation.definitionFit: To slake a thirst is to satisfy or quench it.

clue.text: Edwin departs by the back door

parts.note: D is the timetable abbreviation for departs

indicators.note: by the back means going in reverse, so the word door is read backwards

explanation.surface: A man named Edwin slips out quietly through the rear door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the back' reverses DOOR to ROOD. Edwin Drood is the title character of Dickens's unfinished novel, which also leaves his departure a mystery.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's last, unfinished novel is The Mystery of Edwin Drood, so the first name points to the surname.

clue.text: Aerial producing excellent line

parts.note: A1, written AI, means first-rate or excellent
RY is an abbreviation for railway, a railway line

explanation.surface: A television aerial gives first-rate reception on its line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aerial' looks like the TV antenna noun but is the adjective, of the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerial as an adjective means of the air, light and breezy, the same as the answer.

clue.text: He protested against shortages in Africa

definitions.meaning: The wartime British graffiti figure peering over a wall saying 'Wot, no ...?' about scarce goods
a landlocked country in north-central Africa

explanation.definitionFit: The Chad cartoon complained of rationed goods, and Chad is also a nation found in Africa.

clue.text: Create shaded area for hybrid by hole in the wall

parts.note: a cross is a hybrid of two breeds
a hatch is an opening in a wall, like a serving hatch

explanation.surface: An artist makes shading for a hybrid design beside a gap in the wall.
explanation.definitionFit: To crosshatch is to shade a drawing with intersecting sets of parallel lines.

clue.text: Topping sort of party — embrace and draw close

parts.note: to neck is to kiss and cuddle
to tie is to draw a knot tight and fasten it

explanation.surface: At a terrific party, couples hug and cuddle up close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' sounds like 'excellent' but means hanging: a necktie party is a slang term for a lynching.
explanation.definitionFit: A necktie party is grim slang for a hanging, and topping is British slang for executing someone.

clue.text: See mice in fight with cat, like the pictures

indicators.note: a fight is a scuffle that throws the letters of mice in and cat into disorder

explanation.surface: Watching mice scrap with a cat is just like being at the movies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fight' scrambles MICE IN plus CAT. 'the pictures' is British for the cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: The pictures is old British slang for the cinema, so something like it is filmic.

clue.text: Intelligence and money — a wonderful girl

parts.note: MI is Military Intelligence, as in MI5
the rand is the South African currency

explanation.surface: A girl with brains and wealth seems simply wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: The girl's name comes from Latin mirandus, to be wondered at; Shakespeare's Miranda in The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: The name derives from Latin mirandus, meaning admirable or worthy of wonder.

clue.text: Concede after the bunker on this course

indicators.note: after places the piece for concede behind the piece for the bunker

parts.note: a golf bunker is a sand trap
to own, or own up, is to admit or concede

explanation.surface: A golfer gives up after landing in a bunker on this course.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf surface misleads: Sandown Park is an English horse-racing course in Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandown Park is a racecourse in Surrey, so the answer names a course.

clue.text: Lifted up a second time, painter falls

indicators.note: lifted up in a down clue means the phrase for a second time reads upward

parts.note: again means once more, a second time
RA is a Royal Academician, a painter

explanation.surface: A painter is hoisted up once more, then takes a tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted up' reverses AGAIN to NIAGA, since in a down clue lifting reads the word upward. 'falls' looks like the painter's tumble; it is the waterfall noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Niagara is the great waterfall on the US-Canada border, so the plural noun 'falls' names it.

clue.text: Turns round, odds by prayers

indicators.note: round means one word goes around another

parts.note: veers means changes direction, turns
SP is starting price, the odds offered in betting

explanation.surface: A gambler changes direction, and the odds favour prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' wraps the turning word round the odds. In British betting, starting price is the odds on offer when a race begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Vespers is the evening service of prayers in the church's daily round.

clue.text: Translation almost non-U to Lawrence

indicators.note: almost means drop the last letter

parts.note: non-U, not upper-class, means common or vulgar
T. E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia

explanation.surface: A rendering of a text seems rather common to Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts the R from VULGAR. U and non-U were 1950s British labels for upper-class and common usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vulgate is Jerome's Latin version of the Bible, the standard Latin rendering.

clue.text: Sulks, having deformity

definitions.meaning: the ... in British slang is a fit of sulks, as in having the ...
a rounded bump on the back, a deformity

explanation.definitionFit: Having the hump is British slang for being in a sulk, and a hunched back is a deformity.

clue.text: Rancour heard in France once

indicators.note: heard signals a word that sounds like the word for rancour

parts.note: gall means bitterness, rancour

explanation.surface: Bitterness can be detected in France of old.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaul was the ancient Roman name for the region that is now France.

clue.text: Child, asked, gives her name

indicators.note: gives means the words Child, asked yield a run of letters from within

explanation.surface: A child, when asked, tells someone her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilda is a girl's name, matching the female first name the clue asks for.

clue.text: Faithful private comes up and twice interrupts general

indicators.note: twice means the two letters break into the general's name at two separate places
interrupts means the soldier's letters go inside the general's name

parts.note: General Robert E. Lee, the Confederate commander

indicators.note: comes up in a down clue means the word for a private reads upward

parts.note: GI is an American private soldier

explanation.surface: A loyal private stands up and twice cuts in on the general.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes up' turns the soldier into IG; 'twice interrupts' splits it, I after the general's first letter and G after his next.
explanation.definitionFit: Liege as an adjective means loyal or owing feudal allegiance, as in a liege man.

clue.text: Hurry away from jazz singing

definitions.meaning: ... as a command means go away quickly

explanation.definitionFit: Scat is an order to leave fast, and also improvised nonsense-syllable singing in jazz.

clue.text: Work previously quoted backwards? What a nerve

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: backwards means the abbreviation for previously quoted is read in reverse

parts.note: cit. abbreviates cited, as in op. cit., the work already quoted

explanation.surface: A scholar quotes a work in reverse and is told off for cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backwards' turns CIT into TIC. 'What a nerve' looks like an outburst, but it defines the nerve of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The optic nerve carries signals from the eye to the brain, so it is a kind of nerve.

clue.text: Hate rapid change in social organisation

indicators.note: change means the letters of hate rapid are rearranged

explanation.surface: People hate any sudden change in how society is run.
explanation.definitionFit: Apartheid was South Africa's system of racial segregation, a way of ordering society.

clue.text: Sort of hospital bowl or dish

parts.note: a cottage hospital is a small rural British hospital
in skittles the cheese is the heavy disc that is bowled

explanation.surface: A hospital bowl or dish of some sort.
explanation.walkthrough: A cottage hospital is a small local British hospital; in the pub game of skittles the flat wooden disc thrown is a cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft curd cheese is served as a dish in its own right.
